# Who Pays for Your Medical Care? 

Health insurance isn’t the most exciting subject, but it is easily one of the most important. Here are some key questions to consider and resources you will need when planning for your healthcare coverage.  

## Find out which health insurance is covering you right now
- What is the name of your insurance company
- Is it one of your parent's plans they have through their job? If so, what are the rules for how long you can stay on that plan?
- If you're headed to college, can you get an adequate plan through your school?
- Is your coverage a federal or state-funded insurance (Medicare or Medicaid/MassHealth)? If so, does it change when you get older or if you begin to earn income?

## Find out what your health insurance covers
- Does it cover the doctor you need to see?
- Does it cover the procedure you need to have?
- Does it cover the medications you need to take? 

## Find out what your health insurance costs 
- What is the premium (the amount you pay each month toward the cost of the insurance policy)? 
- Does it have a deductible (the amount you have to pay for your medical care each year before the insurance will begin to cover your costs)? 
- How much are the co-pays (the amount you pay at each visit and for each prescription)? 

## Resources at MGH

### Patient Financial Services (PFS) 
- PFS will work with you if you don’t have enough (or any) insurance coverage. The main number for PFS is [(617) 726-2191](tel:+16177262191). With the passage of new health care legislation, health insurance plans could be changing all the time. You’ll need to keep on top of it to know what the best option is for you.

## What Does Quality & Safety Mean for Your Child?

When you get "outstanding quality" health care, it means your care is based on evidence, family-centered and provided by skilled and knowledgeable professionals who communicate and coordinate the care in a timely way.

You and your child should feel safe at Mass General Brigham for Children, and one of the best ways to improve patient safety is to constantly monitor performance and family experiences to set up systems to provide the best care for your child. The Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety is committed to this work every day.

### High Quality & Safe Care at Mass General Brigham for Children Is:

- Evidence-based
- Family-centered
- Provided by skilled professionals
- Rooted in a culture of open communication and continuous improvement
- Driven by feedback from our families

## About Us

### Our Vision for Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety

Mass General Brigham for Children, as a national leader in Quality and Safety, is distinguished by a culture that partners with patients and families to assure that care is safe, high quality, equitable, and efficient.

This culture is characterized by:

- Teamwork
- Transparency
- Continuous learning and improvement
- Communication
- Innovation

### Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety Core Team

- [Brian Cummings, MD](https://www.massgeneral.org/children/doctors/18255/brian-cummings) — Vice Chair, Medical Director, Mass General Brigham for Children
- Sandra Dodge McGee, MHA — Executive Director, Mass General Brigham for Children and Mass General Brigham Pediatrics
- [Esther Israel, MD](https://www.massgeneral.org/children/doctors/16715/Esther-Israel) — Quality Chair, Pediatrics
- [Cassandra Kelleher, MD](https://www.massgeneral.org/children/doctors/18749/Cassandra-Kelleher) — Quality Chair, Pediatric Surgery
- [Lindsay Carter, MD](https://www.massgeneral.org/children/doctors/18977/Lindsay-Carter) — Director, Inpatient Quality and Safety
- [John Co, MD, MPH](https://www.massgeneral.org/children/doctors/17293/John-Patrick-Co) — Director, Outpatient Quality and Safety
- Kristen Solemina, MPH — Quality and Safety Manager
- Caren Harris, RN, MSN — Quality Nurse Coordinator
- Jessica Mascola, MS — Quality and Safety Program Coordinator
- Cathleen Glynn, RN, MSN — Quality and Safety Data Analyst

### Our History

The Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety Team work with leadership and staff to provide the highest quality, safest and patient-centered care to our families. We strive to create a culture of continuous improvement through communication, education, information dissemination and data-driven improvement.

Since 2009, our team has implemented safety initiatives and evidence-based care models across all care delivery areas at Mass General Brigham for Children.

### Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety Structure

Our structure begins with unit-based triads (physician, nurse and administrator), that report into our ambulatory and inpatient quality and safety team to foster shared learning, teamwork and communication. Our work is driven by priorities set by Mass General Brigham for Children leadership, and MGH leadership including Patient Care Services, Practice Improvement and the MGH Center for Quality and Safety.

## Strategic Plan (5-Year Plan, 2017) — Our Key Areas of Focus

- Reinforce the culture of continuous improvement
- Improve safety culture
- Improve patient safety, especially in high risk areas
- Optimize the patient experience
- Advance provider skills in safety science and quality improvement
- Establish a national presence through scholarly activity

## A Culture of Continuous Improvement

**Strategic Plan, Goal #1: Reinforce the culture of continuous improvement.**

### Quality and Safety Initiatives

Mass General Brigham for Children is engaged in a variety of local and national quality improvement (QI) initiatives, impacting children's health care locally and nationally.

- Every primary care practice, subspecialty division, and inpatient unit is engaged in quality improvement initiatives that they have identified as most meaningful to their patients and themselves. Projects focus on improving different dimensions of care delivery, including patient safety, care effectiveness, patient experience and value.
- To help encourage and support improvement work, Mass General Brigham for Children has developed a Quality and Safety Mini-Grant Program to provide resources and recognition for work initiated by front line care providers. Projects and initiatives are highlighted on the Department's Quality Dashboard, with practices encouraged to present their practice specific data and metrics at division level meetings.
- Mass General Brigham for Children assesses several key quality metrics according to patient/family demographics in an effort to identify and reduce health care disparities.
- At Mass General Brigham for Children, several practices/care units are engaged in quality improvement efforts through national collaboratives, including:
  - Pediatric Gastroenterology — [Improve Care Now](http://www.improvecarenow.org/)
  - Neonatal Intensive Care Unit — [Vermont Oxford Network](https://public.vtoxford.org/)
  - Pediatric Intensive Care Unit — [Pediatric Intensive Care Unit](http://www.myvps.org/)
  - Pediatric Hospitalists Unit — [AAP Value in Inpatient Pediatrics Network Projects](https://www.aap.org/en-us/professional-resources/quality-improvement/Quality-Improvement-Innovation-Networks/Pages/Value-in-Inpatient-Pediatrics-Network-Projects.aspx)
  - Pediatric Surgery — [American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program](https://www.facs.org/quality-programs/childrens-surgery/pediatric/overview)

## Safety Culture / Patient Safety

**Strategic Plan, Goal #2: Improve safety culture.**
**Strategic Plan, Goal #3: Improve patient safety, especially in high risk areas.**

It can be difficult for infants and children to communicate their concerns or changes in symptoms. Mass General Brigham for Children offers our patients, families and staff a robust patient safety program which focuses on family participation in care, mitigation of safety risks, teamwork and rapid response to emergencies. We are committed to being a high reliability organization where our systems support patient safety and allow our patients, families and staff to feel free to speak up about patient safety concerns.

Some examples of our Patient Safety initiatives include:

**Safety Culture** — Mass General Brigham for Children is committed to a strong safety culture in which families and staff feel free to raise patient safety concerns and those voiced concerns result in patient safety improvements. We are proud that we have outperformed our peers on the [AHRQ (Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality)](https://www.ahrq.gov/professionals/quality-patient-safety/patientsafetyculture/index.html) Safety Culture Survey.

**Near Miss Safety Reporting** — Staff are encouraged to report near misses which represent opportunities to improve patient safety. Over 1200 reports are filed across pediatrics every year.

**Medication Safety** — An interdisciplinary medication safety committee, Preventing Pediatric Medication Errors (PPME) Committee, consisting of physicians, nurses, pediatric pharmacists, information systems experts and quality specialists who oversee pediatric medication safety projects.

**Rapid Response** — Mass General Brigham for Children Neonatal and Pediatric Rapid Response Teams can be activated for any acute or unexpected clinical concerns. The Rapid Response Team comes to the patient location to assist patients and care teams with their urgent concerns.

**Good Catch Program** — Mass General Brigham for Children recognizes staff who speak up and prevent an error which could have reached a patient.

**Integrated Electronic Medical Record** — Single electronic medical record across all practices enables all providers to review notes from other providers, test results and medication lists. The patient portal (My Chart) provides patient access to parts of their medical record as well as a secure portal for communicating with their providers.

**[Family-Centered Rounds](https://www.massgeneral.org/assets/MGH/pdf/children/Family_Centered_Rounds.pdf)** — Families are encouraged to participate as team members during morning rounds. This enables parents to actively participate in their child's care planning and provides a time for raising questions or concerns.

## The Patient Experience

Patients and families may receive a phone call or mail survey following their hospitalization or ambulatory visit asking about their experience and anything that we can do better for the family in the future. At Mass General Brigham for Children, we utilize our patient experience survey scores and responses to continually assess the quality of care we provide to our patients and families. Suggestions that families make or improvement opportunities identified allow us to constantly hold ourselves to the highest standards of care for our patients and families.

The Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety team partners with parent volunteers to host staff training sessions. These sessions focus on understanding and optimizing the family experience at Mass General Brigham for Children. Staff gain perspective from the parents as well as strategizing improvement opportunities by directly collaborating with families.

### Patient Experience Survey Comments

> "The staff were amazing. The receptionist is amazing. The nurses are brilliant. My kid just loves it there. Anytime he goes there he feels comfortable, and the staff are unbelievable."

> "They delighted me because they are kind of like an extended family to us. They always treat us with respect. They are always just very courteous. It's just a great experience in stressful times, especially."

> "They were very respectful. They kept us informed on the time of wait. They gave us very good information about the procedure, as well as having very good bedside manner."

> "His ability to sit and talk to a child, engage a child, explain what he was doing, and what was happening. He's a wonderful doctor."

> "[The doctor] is a phenomenal medical doctor, surgeon, and caretaker. He had a kind and wonderful bedside manner with my 11-year-old son. He explained the surgery, was reassuring, and confident. [The doctor] was kind to my son. He patiently listened to questions I had and answered each question. He is the best pediatric surgeon in the world."

> "[The doctor] is the best pediatrician I have ever encountered. She is nice, courteous, great with kids, and has excellent medical knowledge. I have the greatest possible confidence in her abilities to care for our children and have recommended her to numerous friends."

## Quality & Safety Education

**Strategic Plan, Goal #5: Advance provider skills in safety science and quality improvement.**

**[Resident Program](https://www.massgeneral.org/children/pediatric-residency)** — The MGH Pediatric Residency program is committed to educating its trainees in the principles of patient safety and quality improvement, as well as meaningfully engaging residents in improvement initiatives for providing experiential learning opportunities as well as ensuring its initiatives are informed by residents.

- During the first year of the residency program, residents are taught the fundamentals of patient safety and quality improvement by faculty from Mass General Brigham for Children / MGH Quality and Safety leadership.
- By the end of the second year of training, residents are expected to have become a member of and meaningfully participated in a quality improvement initiative at Mass General Brigham for Children.
- The Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety team has implemented "Resident Quality and Safety Rounds," which is a forum for communication between residents and Mass General Brigham for Children Quality and Safety leadership regarding residents' quality and safety concerns.

**Psychological Safety Leadership Programs** — A four-session psychological safety leadership series focused on communication techniques and teamwork.

**[Mass General Brigham's Clinical Process Improvement Leadership Program (CPIP)](http://www.partners.org/Innovation-And-Leadership/Improving-Efficiency-Controlling-Costs/Process-Management.aspx)** — An intensive 6–8 session program with the purpose of engaging clinical teams in the use of process improvement tools to reduce variation in care and improve outcomes for patients.

**[Team STEPPS](https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps/about-teamstepps/index.html)** — An evidence-based teamwork system to improve communication and teamwork skills among health care professionals.

**[Patient Safety Awareness Week](http://www.npsf.org/)** — Mass General Brigham for Children celebrates patient safety accomplishments and educates patients, providers and staff on patient safety. Every year the Mass General location recognizes a select group of [Patient Safety Stars](http://apollo.massgeneral.org/safetystars/), nominated by their peers, for their commitment to patient safety within the hospital.

**Interdisciplinary Tracer Program** — A team consisting of nurses, doctors, physician assistants, registered pharmacists and quality and safety specialists visit each unit to evaluate hospital and patient care operations.

## About Us

For those patients who require its services, our mission is to aid in the critical care post-discharge difficulties that may arise from hospital discharge by providing exceptional service and treatment to the multicultural patients and families we serve. We utilize excellent communication with the family and primary care pediatricians to optimize long-term successful patient outcomes.

The Mass General Brigham for Children PICU provides monitoring and life-sustaining treatment for critically ill patients suffering from a wide range of illnesses. The Mass General Brigham for Children PICU Follow-Up Clinic will focus on evaluating the intensive care patients discharged from the PICU. PICU patients and their families experience a high risk for developing medical, neurodevelopmental, and psychosocial needs related to post-intensive care syndrome. So, it is not uncommon for them to seek out help along this journey. This includes patients who have had a prolonged stay in the PICU for a critical illness.

The Pediatric Intensive Care Unit Follow-Up Clinic is a developmental follow-up service. We support your children through the aid in their development, growth, and recovery for them to reach their full potential.

These issues have commonly been overlooked by health care providers as post-intensive care patients transition care back into the community following their serious illness. The Mass General Brigham for Children PICU Follow-Up Clinic was uniquely designed to combat this issue.

This process can be described in four steps:

## Steps of Patient Care

1. Hospital discharge
2. Evaluate areas of cognition and psychosocial function
3. Neurodevelopment and family functioning to identify ongoing needs, and set up referrals to community providers for ongoing follow-up
4. Support the child and family through the long-term recovery after critical illness

en.description: Why vaccines matter for your child and your community — answers to common parent questions.

content.markdown:
Vaccines can help prevent many diseases that affect children and adults. Some parents are nervous about their children getting vaccines, and that's okay. In this resource, you will learn why vaccines are important for your child's health and your community's health.

## Why should my child get vaccinated?

Vaccines help prevent many diseases that affect children and adults. This includes diseases that are not common, like measles, mumps and rubella, rotavirus and polio. These diseases used to be common, but now they are not — because most children and adults have been vaccinated.

## Why does my child need so many vaccines when they are young?

We give children vaccines as early as possible to protect them from disease. It might seem like a lot, but there is enough time in between each vaccine or dose so your child can build up immunity (resistance) to the disease.

Delaying your child's vaccines means delaying protection against disease. Talk with your child's doctor if you have questions or concerns about your child's vaccine schedule (the time between vaccines).

## How well do vaccines work?

Most vaccines work about 90% of the time. This means that **9 out of 10 children** who get a vaccine will not catch the disease the vaccine protects against. Not every vaccine works all of the time, but many work well for children and adults.

## Do vaccines cause autism?

**No.** Studies have not been able to show that vaccines cause autism. The one study that showed vaccines cause autism was retracted (proven to be untrue). The doctor who did that study lost his medical license. Many more studies with large numbers of children have been done since then. These studies haven't shown a connection between vaccines and autism.

## I'm nervous about my child getting their vaccines. What can I do?

Talk with your child's doctor about your concerns or questions. They can tell you more about each vaccine, why it's important, and how it can help your child.

## How does vaccinating my child help others?

- **It helps protect children and adults who can't get vaccinated.** There are some children who can't get vaccinated for medical reasons. When your child is vaccinated, it helps protect other children or adults who can't.
- **It helps lower the number of people affected by a disease.** As more people are vaccinated against a certain disease, the disease affects fewer people over time. For example, measles used to affect children in the United States. Now, there are very few families in the U.S. who are affected by measles. This is because most children are vaccinated against measles.

> 9 out of every 10 people who get a vaccine will not catch the disease they are vaccinated against.

en.description: Room-by-room tips to make your home safer before your baby starts crawling.

content.markdown:
It is exciting when your baby learns to crawl and walk. This is an important time to make your home as safe as possible for your baby. In this resource, you will learn how to childproof your home before your baby learns to crawl.

## What is childproofing your home?

When you childproof your home, you make your home as safe as possible for when your baby arrives. How you childproof your home changes as your baby grows up.

## How long does it take to childproof my home?

Babyproofing changes over time. As your baby grows and develops new skills, you will need to adjust the level of safety in your home.

## How do I childproof my home before my baby learns to crawl?

Babies like to grab onto surfaces, pick up objects, and put them in their mouths. They learn to understand the world around them through touch and taste. Here are tips to childproof your home:

### Kitchen

- When you cook or prepare food, keep your baby in a highchair or safely enclosed play area where you can see them.
- Install locks or stops on drawers, cabinets, switches, the refrigerator door, and oven doors. Keep magnets and other small objects out of your baby's reach.
- Turn pot handles inward on the stove. Use the burners toward the back wall.
- Store household cleaners and poisons in locked cabinets that are out of your baby's reach.
- Keep small appliances and other items away from the edges of countertops or tables.

### Living room, den, and bedrooms

- Attach televisions and heavy furniture, like bookshelves, to the wall. This can help prevent the TV or furniture from falling if your baby bumps into it or pushes on it.
- Secure and hide electrical cords.
- If you have older children, have them put away their toys out of your baby's reach.
- Keep the floors and other surfaces free of items your baby could choke on or break.

### Bathroom and laundry room

- Secure toilet lids.
- Store cleaners, poisons, and laundry products in a locked cabinet out of your child's reach.
- Empty the bathtub or other large containers with liquid as soon as you are done using them.

### Other tips

- Use safety covers in electrical outlets.
- Install safety gates at the top and bottom of every staircase.
- Cover sharp corners on furniture or household objects.
- For more tips, ask the care team or visit the [National Safety Council's childproofing page](https://www.nsc.org/home-safety/safety-topics/child-safety/childproofing).

> **Did you know?** The best way to childproof your home is to see the world from your baby's point of view. Get down on the floor — or as close as possible — to check for anything your baby could get into.

en.description: Distracted driving causes more than half of teen crashes — what families should know about the law and good habits.

content.markdown:
Driver distraction is responsible for **more than 58% of teen automobile crashes**. Michael Flaherty, DO, of the Pediatric Trauma Service and the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) at MGHfC shares these tips to keep drivers, their families, and the community safe.

## Key Takeaways

- Set mobile electronic devices to **Do Not Disturb** mode, which prevents texts, calls, and notifications from coming through while the user is in a vehicle.
- Set an example for others. Peers, children, and colleagues learn from one another, so we need to make distracted driving an unacceptable behavior.
- Talk with your teenage driver about the dangers of driving while distracted — including the risks of using cell phones, eating, and manipulating the radio while behind the wheel. Remind teens that driving requires all of their attention.

## What is distracted driving?

Distracted driving means your attention or focus is taken away from the task of driving. It comprises three core types:

- **Visual** — when you take your eyes off the road
- **Manual** — when you take your hands off the wheel
- **Cognitive** — when your mind is not primarily focused on driving

Distracted driving is dangerous and can lead to injury and death. **More than 1,000 people are injured daily in crashes involving a distracted driver.** While any distraction can endanger the driver and others, texting while driving is especially dangerous as it combines all three types of distraction. It takes the brain approximately 30 seconds to refocus on driving after looking at a mobile phone.

## What is the law?

The Massachusetts hands-free law prohibits all drivers from all use of their phones, for any reason — including making calls, reading or sending text messages, using social media, or typing in directions — even when at a stop light or in traffic.

## What if I need to use navigation, answer the phone, or make a call?

Drivers can use their mobile device's voice commands for directions and calls — such as Apple's Siri or Google Assistant — which must be enabled to place calls or get directions. Cars without built-in GPS, Apple CarPlay, or Android Auto must be equipped with a phone mount on the dash or windshield for GPS navigation. Drivers must type in their destination and start the directions **before** driving.

If you need to answer or make a phone call, the safest thing to do is pull over to the side of the road or park your car in a safe location.

## What should parents do?

Drivers under the age of 20 have the highest rate of distraction-related fatal crashes. Parents need to foster open conversations about the importance of the law and how it works to ensure their own safety and the safety of others.

Since 2010 it has been illegal in Massachusetts for any junior operator — drivers under age 18 — to talk on the phone in any way while driving, including hands-free.

Encourage teenage drivers to speak up if they see their peers or others driving distracted, just as they would if someone were driving drunk. Parents must also set good examples by not using their phones while driving.

en.description: Age-appropriate ways to talk with kids — toddlers to teens — about gun violence and home gun safety.

content.markdown:
*By Gretchen Fischer Felopulos, PhD, and Gene Beresin, Executive Director — MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds*

Recent mass shootings that have made national news headlines are a frightening reminder to us all of this "new normal." Beyond those that have made national headlines, there are many more incidents of gun violence — sometimes more than one a day — for which the trauma is felt only locally.

We emotionally respond to these horrifying incidents with a sense of terror, fear for our own safety, and sadness for the victims and those who loved them. We ask ourselves: was it yet another random act of violence by a troubled individual, or was it inspired by hateful voices that fueled the flames of someone who felt alone, angry, and marginalized?

Beyond our immediate gut reactions, we can expect media coverage to extend across our televisions, radios, computers, and mobile devices, as in any crisis. And we can expect that our kids, teenagers, and young adults will have varying levels of information about these tragic events, along with their own emotional reactions, questions, and concerns.

How can parents, educators, and other caring adults help our young people process acts of gun violence in this moment, when we know they already feel vulnerable? How can we help them live with confidence and self-assurance in the world without constant fear that their everyday life is filled with imminent danger? How can we help them put these tragedies into some perspective?

As with any of our caregiver guidelines, first remember that you know your child best. Then, the approach for each child should be developmentally appropriate. What helps a 7-year-old cope with fear and anxiety may not be the same for a 17-year-old.

Below are some basic tips for how to talk with a child of any age about gun violence.

## Talking Tips for All Ages

**Control your own anxiety.** Let's face it — we are all scared about gun violence. Anxiety is contagious, and your kids will know this. If they ask you directly, be honest and say you are rattled by recent shootings, and express how terrible you feel for these losses and for the victims' families and communities.

**Use self-care measures to calm yourself down.** Research shows that when a parent is calm and under control, they are in the best position to talk with their kids about scary things.

**Talk with other adults you trust about gun violence and hate crimes.** Sometimes partners, friends, family, clergy, or community leaders will help you clarify your own reactions and help you contain your anxiety.

**Be proactive.** Limit your own exposure to gun violence by turning off the news coverage and avoiding social media posts focused on violent events. While it is important to stay informed, repeatedly viewing the news stories and related content tends to add to our fears, not reduce them.

**Keep your own home safe from gun violence.** Around one in three homes with children contains at least one firearm, so it is critical for gun-owning parents to safely store them away — ideally by locking up the unloaded gun and storing the ammunition in a separate locked location. If you think your children don't know where you keep your guns, or that they know not to play with them, think again. Research and past experience have shown that too many accidental shootings occur in the home by making these assumptions.

**Talk with your kids about gun safety rules.** If you have guns in the home, be sure to talk with your children of any age about gun safety rules. No child should be able to have any access to firearms without adult supervision. If you have not developed and discussed family rules about the storage, access, and use of firearms, establish them, post them, and have a serious conversation about your rules. Even if you don't have guns in your home, it is possible that there are firearms at a friend's home — so it is key that you talk with your young people about gun safety. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that you ask parents about their own gun safety practices before your child attends a playdate, party, or sleepover at their home.

## Talking Tips by Age Group

### Toddlers and Preschoolers

**Very young children are more disturbed by their parents' and caregivers' distress than by the actual event.** They may not fully understand what happened, or they may see it as more than an act on TV. That's why they're comforted more by your actions than your words. Be careful how you present yourself to them, both emotionally and in conversation with others. Naturally, they will pick up on your reactions.

**Expect young children to regress a bit emotionally.** They may become clingy or whiny, have difficulty sleeping, or start wetting their beds. The more patient and reassuring you are, the more quickly these episodes will pass.

**Turn off the media.** Young children have no idea where distant cities are, and may think the events happened right near their homes. Let them know that these places are far away. If you wish to watch or listen to news coverage, do so while your very young children are not in the room; they do not yet have the ability to put the frightening images they see into perspective. If you have conversations about shootings with a partner or older children at home, be sure they are not within earshot.

### Grade School Children

**Encourage your school-aged children to share their feelings and concerns with you.** Certainly, they will have heard about recent events. Assure them that it's all right for them to be upset, and that you'll do everything you can to protect them from harm.

**Ask what specifically worries them** and what they know about recent shootings. Also, ask where they heard about it — it is very important to know where they get their information.

**If appropriate, reassure them that you live in a very safe place** and that these events are not common — though you do need to admit that they are very scary.

**Remember that children often work through emotional issues with play instead of words.** Don't be surprised if your children use toys to replay the images they've seen or imagined. This is healthy. It can also give you insights into their fears and misunderstandings.

**Expect that your children might ask the same questions several times.** Be patient. By asking these questions, they're showing you that they trust you and what you say.

**Turn off the media.** It is not wise for school-aged kids to follow news coverage of these events. However, if they have already seen or heard about the breaking news, be available to clarify their concerns.

**Remind them:** there are more good people in the world than there are bad people, and the good people will always try to take care of and protect them.

**Talk about angry feelings and how to manage them.** Even school-aged kids know that children and adults get angry and have conflicts, and they have probably seen all sorts of violence in movies, on TV, and in real life. Discuss how anger can be managed, and explain that there is never reason to manage anger with violence.

### Teenagers and Young Adults

Adolescents may be scared and wonder what this means for the lives they'll lead as young adults. For example, "Will I be safe in college, or in the community where I live and work?" They may struggle with questions about justice, power, and the use of weapons — issues that directly relate to violent events. And as parents, young people of color or other marginalized individuals may be particularly worried.

Teenagers are capable of having nuanced discussions and considering issues, values, motives, and consequent behavior — appropriate and unacceptable.

**Let your teenagers listen as you discuss the event with other adults.** If they choose to chime in, welcome their participation — even if you might disagree with what they have to say. Simply talking things out will help them to put their concerns into perspective.

**Sit with them as they watch the news coverage.** Comment on what you're seeing, and listen openly to what they have to say, as well. Encourage them to limit their time spent on related content — for many people, this only adds to their fears.

**Share your feelings with them.** This gives adolescents permission to do the same with you. Share your feelings about mass shootings, the targets of the shootings, and issues with use and misuse of firearms. Ask about their feelings about these issues.

**Discuss the risks of access to guns.** Teens are capable of discussing how many guns we have in our nation and whether this is safe or dangerous for society, as well as talking about factors that contribute to gun violence — such as domestic abuse, drugs and alcohol, and mental health issues like depression. Access to a gun is one of the biggest risk factors on the list. Engage in conversations about how reduction of firearms and "red flag" laws have been shown to prevent personal violence (suicide) and reduce rates of homicide and mass shootings.

**Talk with them about appropriate gun use and gun safety.** Teens are old enough to appreciate that firearms in the hands of an angry, impulsive person are dangerous. Talk with them about the appropriate use of firearms — such as for hunting, skeet shooting, target shooting, and on rare occasions, for self-defense.

**Ask them about their opinion on assault rifles.** Talk with them about why anyone would use one. They are not used for hunting or for sport. Is there any time or reason someone would need to use one?

**Ask them about their opinion of copycat phenomena.** Wonder with them about how media coverage of shootings affects people's feelings, and whether they think some might copy the event, or react negatively.

**Wonder about risks to people of color.** Research shows that people of color are at a much greater risk of being shot or killed by guns. Ask your teens and young adults how people of color, Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, and other marginalized people such as the LGBTQ population are at greater risk for violence of all sorts.

---

We desperately need to keep our children and society safe. We need action to prevent more devastating events. With 40,000 gun-related deaths in our country per year, this is a public health crisis and our children are at risk.

One important role we have in preventing needless death by firearms — besides state and national legislation — is having conversations with our youth to help them feel safe and be part of the solution when they become leaders in the future.

title: Guardianship: What You Need to Know

en.description: How guardianship works for adults over 18 who are incapacitated — types of guardians, alternatives, and effects on health care.

content.markdown:
You may have many questions about guardianship and health care. In this resource, you will learn how guardianship affects health care for adults over age 18 who are incapacitated. You will also learn about the different types of guardians and related roles.

## What is a legal guardian?

A legal guardian is a person (or people) named by the Probate and Family Court who is responsible for another adult's support, protection, and wellbeing when the court finds that an adult is incapacitated (cannot make informed decisions for themselves). This includes decisions around major areas of life, like medical care and housing. The court might also name a legal conservator. This person makes decisions around legal paperwork. Both guardians and conservators help the adult in their care with public benefits and services, general welfare, and planning for the future.

## Which paperwork gives the details of guardianship?

The Probate and Family Court provides the legal paperwork. The paperwork is called the **Decree and Order**. It includes information about the guardian and/or conservator, and the limits of their roles.

## At what age does a child become their own legal guardian?

Children become their own legal guardians at age 18. This means they are legal adults — even if they are incapacitated. For this reason, it is important to get legal guardianship before the person turns 18 if they are incapacitated.

## Why does an adult need a guardian?

Adults need a guardian when the court finds that the person is incapacitated. This means they cannot make informed decisions on their own.

To be incapacitated, adults must:

- Be at least 18 years old
- Have a doctor's diagnosis of incapacitation
- Be unable to assess or communicate medical information or make decisions for themselves

## Are there limitations to guardianship?

Yes. These limitations might let a person make decisions in certain areas, but not others. The court gives a list of the limitations with the Decree and Order paperwork.

There are some situations that need more permission from the Probate and Family Court. These include:

- Major surgery involving general anesthesia
- Being admitted to a residential (live-in) facility
- Being given antipsychotic medications or needing complex medical treatment

## How does guardianship affect health care?

Guardianship affects how information is written in medical records. It also affects how medical decisions are made and who the care team can talk to.

- **Documentation in medical records.** The care team needs a copy of the most recent guardianship paperwork. This paperwork is kept in the medical record.
- **Medical decisions.** The care team follows the process for medical decision-making written in the guardianship paperwork. As the guardian, you must tell the care team if anything changes.
- **Communication.** The care team follows the process for communicating written in the guardianship paperwork. As the guardian, you must tell the care team if anything changes.

## Types of legal guardians

There are many types of legal guardians. Each type has its own set of rules listed in the Letters of Appointment and Decree and Order. The most common types are:

- **Plenary** — also called a full or general guardian. A plenary can make all medical care decisions for an adult.
- **Limited guardian** — can only make decisions that are authorized by the court and listed in the paperwork.
- **Temporary guardian** — the court can name a temporary guardian in an emergency when there is a strong chance that an adult can make their own decisions in the future. Courts decide on a temporary guardian on a case-by-case basis.
- **Co-guardian** — shares guardianship with another legal guardian.
- **Rogers Monitor** — responsible for following the court-approved treatment plan for the use of antipsychotic medication prescribed to the person under guardianship.
- **Guardian ad Litem (GAL)** — reports to the court on any recommendations related to future guardianship decisions.
- **Guardianship of a minor** — the court might name a legal guardian for a child under 18 whose parents cannot or will not make medical decisions. This guardian makes decisions about the child's health, education, and safety.

## Alternatives to guardianship

Decisions about a person's health care, wellbeing, personal items, or finances may legally be made by someone other than the person, their parent, or legal guardian.

These alternatives include:

- **Health care proxy.** An adult can name someone else (called an *agent*) to make health care decisions when they temporarily cannot do so.
- **Durable Power of Attorney (DPOA).** A person named as DPOA can make certain legal and financial decisions for the person who names them. A DPOA is just for legal and financial decisions — it cannot be used to make health care decisions.
- **Conservator.** A conservator manages the finances, property, and belongings of a person who needs financial protection. They also make legal decisions. The conservator must be named by the Probate and Family Court. A person can be a conservator and a guardian at the same time. A conservator who is not also a guardian cannot make medical decisions.

## Where can I learn more about guardianship?

- Your lawyer or legal team
- [Massachusetts laws on guardianship and conservatorship](https://www.mass.gov/topics/guardianship)
- [Probate and Family Court Forms](https://www.mass.gov/guides/probate-and-family-court-forms)
- [Massachusetts Guardianship Association](http://www.massguardianshipassociation.org/)

---

*Rev. 3/2018. This document is intended to provide health-related information so that you may be better informed. It is not a substitute for a doctor's medical advice and should not be relied upon for treatment for specific medical conditions.*

en.description: Apps and phone tricks to help you remember when to take your medicine, especially once you're managing it on your own.

content.markdown:
As you become more independent, you may need to take your medicine without your parents reminding you. College, work, and being away from home can make it difficult to remember. It can also be difficult to remember your medicine if you are feeling well.

This resource offers smartphone apps that remind you to take your medicine.

## Why set up smartphone reminders?

- Cell phone reminders help people remember to take their medicine.
- Reminders decrease the rate of health complications.

## How do smartphone reminders work?

- If you have a calendar app on your phone, you can program it to send texts to you at the times you need to take your medicine. These texts can be labeled with the names of your medicines and the dosages. There are also dedicated apps that send you text reminders.
- Some apps include back-up alerts to a parent or any other person of your choice. These alerts are sent only if you do not check in after receiving your text reminder.
- Some apps keep track of how often you check in, so you can print and give the record to your doctor.
- Some apps remind you to refill your prescription.

## Free smartphone apps

- [**Medisafe Virtual Pillbox**](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.medisafe.android.client) — Google Play
- [**Pill Monitor**](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/pill-monitor-drug-minder/id485247638) — Apple App Store

Other apps can be found by searching the App Store or Google Play for terms like *"medication reminder"*.

## How can I make my reminders private?

Give your medicine reminders **code names** if you are concerned about other people seeing your reminders. Keep a key of what the messages mean in a separate, safe place.

title: Navigating Relationships with a Chronic Illness

en.description: How a chronic illness can shape your relationships with friends, family, and partners — and how to handle the conversations.

content.markdown:
Sometimes your medical problems can affect other parts of your life. This may come up with friends, family, and dating. Read more to learn how you can enjoy your various relationships.

## Friends

When deciding whether to tell a friend about your medical condition, think about:

- Your personality type and what feels comfortable to you
- Your friend's personality
- The closeness and type of friendship you share

Friends can be a great source of support. They will often feel grateful that you've chosen to tell them something so personal.

However, some friends may not understand the health challenges you have to deal with, and this can make it tough to connect with them. When people make insensitive comments, they may not understand, they may be afraid, or they may not know what to do. Sometimes sharing your experience with them may help them understand and make it easier for them to ask you questions.

People may still not get it. If this happens, only you will know whether it's a relationship to keep or one that is better to let go of. This can be hard. Your family or healthcare team — doctor, psychiatrist, nutritionist, social worker — can help you sort this out.

For the most part, though, friends can be a great source of support, and will often be really impressed by how much you're juggling.

## Family

Typically parents are very involved when you are first diagnosed with a medical condition as a kid or teenager. This is because your parents want to make sure you're safe and as healthy as you can be. It's also because your medical team asked them to make sure you took your medications, ate a healthy diet, and made it to your medical appointments.

Many young adults find it helpful to have family members continue to support them with their care. The downside, however, is that your parents can seem over-protective, or you might become too dependent.

Parents may still want to know what's going on with your care. After all, they're your parents — so they naturally worry and want the best for you. Sometimes their "nagging" comes from a place of caring concern, and that's important to keep in mind. When you're starting to feel frustrated, try talking to your parents. Being open about your feelings can sometimes avoid arguments. Your confidence and good decision-making can have a big impact on helping to ease your parents' concerns.

In addition to your parents, it can be helpful to talk to brothers and sisters. When someone has a medical condition it can affect the entire family — including your siblings, who may be going through their own range of emotions. Siblings often feel more protective of you, closer to you, and may really understand what you're dealing with. They may also feel guilt, anger, fear, or feel like they're being ignored. Talking to your siblings directly may help you have a better understanding of where each of you is coming from.

And don't forget that your healthcare team can help you as well.

## Dating

Just like with friends, you may struggle with if, when, or what to say about your medical condition to someone you're dating. There may be physical signs that you worry the person you are dating may see. This might make you feel insecure and less confident about yourself.

Ultimately, the person who decides what to tell their partner is **you**. Trust yourself. You will have a sense for when it's time. Your partner doesn't need all the details — only as much as you're comfortable sharing. And just as you needed time to understand your condition, try to allow them the same.

And don't forget: your family and healthcare team are there for you at any point along the way.

title: Bronchitis: What You Need to Know

en.description: Acute bronchitis affects the airways and usually clears on its own — what to watch for, when to call the doctor.

content.markdown:
Acute bronchitis is an illness that affects the bronchial tubes, or airways. Learn about acute bronchitis and its symptoms.

## What is acute bronchitis?

Acute bronchitis, or simply bronchitis, is a condition in which the bronchial tubes (airways) become swollen and inflamed. The swelling and inflammation can make it harder to breathe. It is called *acute* bronchitis because the illness lasts only a few weeks.

## What causes acute bronchitis?

**Viruses** (a certain type of germ) are the most common cause of acute bronchitis. Other causes include:

- Bacteria
- Fungal (fungus) infections
- Spending time around things that can bother your airways, such as dust, chemicals, or smoke

## What is the difference between viruses and bacteria?

**Bacteria** can live in many different types of environments. There are good bacteria and bad bacteria. Infections caused by bad bacteria often get better with antibiotics.

**Viruses** are germs that multiply once a small number of virus germs enter your body. Infections caused by viruses do not usually get better with antibiotics.

## What are the symptoms of acute bronchitis?

Symptoms of acute bronchitis usually last about 2–3 weeks. Symptoms can also look similar to other illnesses, like a cold or the flu.

Common symptoms include:

- Cough with yellow or green phlegm (mucus)
- Shortness of breath or wheezing (a whistling sound when you breathe in)
- Fever or chills
- Body or muscle aches
- Sore throat

## How do doctors test for acute bronchitis?

A doctor might use one or more of the following tests for acute bronchitis:

- Physical exam
- Review of your child's medical history
- Chest X-ray
- Pulse oximetry (a test that measures how much oxygen is in your child's blood)
- Test of the mucus from the lungs or nose

## How do doctors treat acute bronchitis?

Treatment depends on your child's symptoms and age. If your child's acute bronchitis is caused by a virus, they should get better on their own with rest and fluids. The doctor will talk with you about which treatments are right for your child.

In most cases, **antibiotics will not help your child feel better.** Acute bronchitis is usually caused by a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria, but not viruses.

## When should I call the doctor?

Call the doctor if your child's symptoms do not get better after 2–3 weeks, or if their symptoms get worse.

---

en.description: Know-your-rights basics for non-citizens — finding a lawyer, ICE encounters, hospital protections, and sanctuary cities.

content.markdown:
> ⚠️ **This resource was last updated February 2017.** Immigration policy and enforcement practices have changed since then. Use this as a starting point, but consult an immigration lawyer or current legal-aid resource for up-to-date guidance.

If you do not have a current legal immigration status, we strongly encourage you to talk with an experienced immigration lawyer.

## Find an Immigration Lawyer

- **Boston-area FREE immigration clinics**
  - Boston Residents: the [Mayor's Office of New Bostonians](https://www.cityofboston.gov/newbostonians/programs/advice.asp) offers monthly free immigration clinics. See website for schedule.
  - [Irish International Immigrant Center (IIIC)](https://iiicenter.org/) — free immigration clinic for immigrants from any country.
- [Mass Legal Services — Find Legal Aid](http://www.masslegalservices.org/FindLegalAid)
- [Mass Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition (MIRA)](https://www.miracoalition.org/) — call **617-350-5480** and ask for their list of immigration lawyers.

## Know Your Rights

Make sure you and others know what to do if an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent stops you.

**You have a right to remain silent — whatever your immigration status.** You can refuse to speak to an ICE agent. Do not answer any questions, especially about your birth place, immigration status, or how you entered the United States.

There are **rights cards** that you can carry with you that say in English that you want to remain silent and that you want to speak with a lawyer. Carry a rights card with you. Download a card from:

content.label: National Immigration Law Center — Everyone Has Certain Basic Rights
ILRC Red Cards

content.markdown:
If ICE agents approach you on the street, ask if you are free to leave. If the agents say yes, calmly and silently walk away. If the agents say no, say you want to remain silent and to speak with a lawyer (or show them your rights card).

**You have the right to see a warrant** before letting anyone into your home. Slide your rights card under the door. Do not open the door unless an ICE agent shows you a warrant signed by a judge with the correct name and address of the person they are looking for on it. Ask them to slip the warrant under the door or show it to you through a window before you open the door.

**You have the right to speak with a lawyer and the right to make a phone call.** Make sure to carry the phone number for an immigration lawyer with you. You have the right to refuse to sign anything before you talk to a lawyer. You have the right to refuse to show any documents before you talk to a lawyer. **Never lie or give false information** to an immigration agent or police officer. Do not carry false identity cards or papers with you.

## Make a Safety Plan

These websites offer helpful tips:

- [ILRC Community Resources](https://www.ilrc.org/community-resources) and [Know Your Rights and What Immigrant Families Should Do Now](https://www.ilrc.org/know-your-rights-and-what-immigrant-families-should-do-now) — available in Spanish and Chinese
- [American Friends Service Committee — Know Your Rights](https://www.afsc.org/) — available in Spanish
- [Immigrant Defense Project — ICE Home and Community Arrests](http://www.immdefense.org/ice-home-and-community-arrests/) — available in 8 languages

## Your Rights in the Hospital

Most of the time ICE agents are supposed to avoid sensitive locations such as hospitals and doctors' offices — also schools, places of worship, weddings and funerals, and public demonstrations. ICE agents can enter these places if they get a supervisor's approval, or in situations related to national security, terrorism, or public safety, or where there is an imminent risk of destruction of evidence in an ongoing criminal case.

*The new President could change this policy to allow agents to enter sensitive locations more freely.*

For more information see: [DHS — Frequently Asked Questions on Existing Guidance for Enforcement Actions](https://www.dhs.gov/news/2016/07/15/fact-sheet-frequently-asked-questions-existing-guidance-enforcement-actions-or).

## Sanctuary Cities Offer Protection — But Not As Much as You May Think

Sanctuary status is meant to build trust between immigrants and local police. Rules vary, but typically local police in sanctuary cities will not ask victims or witnesses about their immigration status, and will not hold immigrants charged with minor crimes for ICE after they would otherwise be released.

Don't be confused by the word *"sanctuary."* Immigration laws are still in force in these places. It's just that the federal government has to enforce the laws — not the local police.

Some colleges offer sanctuary to their undocumented students. If the federal government says *"give me the names of your non-citizens,"* the colleges can refuse. But if ICE returns with a warrant, the colleges will have to provide the information.

Source for this section: [The Boston Globe — What is a sanctuary city?](https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2017/01/27/what-sanctuary-city/8mXFmc9TZUPZhBZhn1Mi6H/story.html)

---

title: Healthy Sleep Habits for Your Baby

en.description: Build a consistent bedtime routine, follow safe-sleep guidelines, and help your baby learn to fall asleep on their own.

content.markdown:
It is hard to imagine, but you will get a full night of uninterrupted sleep again. This resource provides tips to help build healthy sleep habits for your baby so you will all get better sleep.

## Why is this important?

Most babies do not figure out how to be "good" sleepers on their own. It is a process that takes time, patience, and practice — just like many other things as our children grow. Illness can sometimes lead to setbacks where you need to adjust the sleep routine. Keep an open mind and remember that if you can build healthy sleep habits from the start, you are moving in the right direction.

## When should we start?

A baby's sleep pattern begins to change around 3–4 months old as they start to have sleep cycles more like adults. Babies can have trouble staying asleep between sleep cycles. This is a good time to work with your baby on self-soothing strategies, so when they wake up in the middle of the night, they have the skills to get back to sleep without your help.

## Sleep associations

Spend some time observing your baby's sleep patterns — including when they typically nap and when they sleep longer at night. Do they typically need to be held or rocked to fall asleep? Do they usually fall asleep while feeding?

If you answered "yes" to the questions above, your baby has developed a sleep association that involves needing **you** to fall asleep. Teaching new sleep associations that don't require you to step in will help.

## Routines and sleep environment

Try to create a calm and consistent bedtime routine around the same time every night. This will help signal to your baby that it is time to wind down.

If your baby always falls asleep on the bottle or breast, consider feeding them outside of the bedroom to try to remove the association of feeding and sleeping. If they typically fall asleep while feeding before even getting to the bedtime routine, consider moving the feeding time up a bit earlier.

When it is bedtime:

- Set a comfortable room temperature (**68–72°F**)
- Turn down the lights
- Minimize loud noises — consider a white noise machine if your house is noisy

Try some bedtime activities after the last feed — a warm bath, baby massage, reading a story, or singing the same song. Try to do things in the same order each night. Be sure all caretakers follow the same routine. **Consistency is key.**

## Safe sleep guidelines

Follow the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommendations for safe sleep to lower the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS):

- Put your baby to sleep on their back on a firm mattress
- Avoid soft bedding or bumpers
- Share a room, but not the bed
- Stop swaddling and switch to a wearable sleep sack as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll over

## Awake but drowsy

Finding the right time to put your baby to sleep in the crib is very important. A key phrase you'll see repeated in sleep resources is **"awake but drowsy"** — putting your baby to bed when they are tired or ready to sleep but still awake.

Watch for cues during the bedtime routine that your baby is getting tired. You may notice a lowered activity level, less eye contact, or eye rubbing. This is the best time to put your baby in the bassinet or crib — before they get overtired and fussy.

If your baby cries when you put them in the crib, you might try singing a song or saying "I love you" and then walking out of the room. Use the same reassuring song or words night after night.

Crying is natural but can be hard to hear. Set a timer and wait a few minutes before checking in again. If you need to go back in, try not picking them up — you might pat them or sing the song again. With each night sticking to the same routine, your baby will learn to fall asleep on their own.

Remember: it is **much easier** to teach this to a 4–5 month-old than to an older baby or toddler.

## Wake windows and naps

**Sleep often begets sleep.** Timing naps and bedtime is key. Try to get a sense of your baby's *wake window* — the amount of time that your baby is awake before they start to get tired. This will vary by age and is typically **1.5–3 hours** for 2- to 4-month-olds. If you wait too long and miss the window, your baby will start to get overtired and will be harder to put to sleep.

Also, watch out for long, late afternoon naps. These may make it harder for your baby to be ready to sleep at bedtime.

A baby who learns to fall asleep at night on their own is more likely to fall back asleep on their own if they wake up, so work on "awake but drowsy" first.

## Night awakenings

It is normal for sleepers, even adults, to briefly wake up at night as they go through their sleep cycles. A baby that "sleeps through the night" is a baby that falls back to sleep quietly in the middle of the night without crying out for their caregiver.

If your baby wakes up at night, give them a few minutes to see if they can fall back to sleep on their own. If your baby can see you from the crib, consider installing a physical barrier like a curtain to remove the visual contact. If you go to your baby, keep the room dark and avoid talking and eye contact — so your baby doesn't think it is playtime. Be gentle and reassuring.

Remember that your baby won't learn to sleep better right away, and there is not one perfect method to teach them. The goal is to help your baby feel calm with less of your involvement over time. Talk to your baby's pediatrician if you need help.

## More resources

**Websites**

- [HealthyChildren.org](https://www.healthychildren.org) (AAP) — search *"Getting Your Baby to Sleep"* and *"Self-Soothing: Help Your Baby Learn This Life Skill"*
- [ZeroToThree.org](https://www.zerotothree.org) — search *"sleep"*
- [BabySleep.com — Advice by Child Age](https://www.babysleep.com/advice/by-child-age)
- [Dr. Craig Canapari](https://drcraigcanapari.com)

en.description: Drowning is the leading cause of unintentional death in MA kids — swim skills, supervision, pool gates, and CPR.

content.markdown:
Going for a swim in the pool or lake is a great way to keep cool in the summer heat. While taking a dip in the water is a lot of fun, it's important to know how to prevent children from drowning. **Drowning is the leading cause of unintentional injury and death in children ages 0–14 in Massachusetts.** Here are some tips for preventing drowning when your children go for a swim.

## How can I prevent my younger child from drowning?

For babies, younger children, and people who have less experience swimming, it's important to have an adult nearby who knows how to swim and can watch for danger. Also follow these tips:

- **Make sure your child learns how to swim.** If your child knows how to swim, they will be safer and more confident in the water — whether it's a pool, lake, or other body of water.
- **Learn how to swim if you don't know how.** If you know how to swim, you can help teach your child how to swim and stay safe in the water. You can also help your child if they are ever in danger.
- **Never leave your child alone in the water — even for a moment.** You should always be an arm's length away from your child in the water, including a bathtub. Your child can drown in even a few inches of water if they are not watched carefully.
- **Learn CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation).** CPR is a lifesaving technique that can help your child or others who are near drowning. Many schools or community centers, like your local YMCA, offer classes to learn CPR.

> **Did you know?** When a child is drowning, it's often silent and happens very quickly. Children don't splash or yell for help when drowning, like you'd see on TV or in a movie. Children can go underwater quickly — especially in strong currents like the ocean. If you notice your child is missing, check the water first to see if they went underwater.

## How can I prevent my older child from drowning?

For older children, teenagers, and people with more experience swimming, it's still important to have an adult nearby who knows how to swim and can watch for danger. Also follow these tips:

- **Make sure your child learns how to swim.** If your child knows how to swim, they will be safer and more confident in the water.
- **Learn how to swim if you don't know how.** You can help teach your child to swim and stay safe in the water, and help them if they are ever in danger.
- **If your older child knows how to swim, have them swim with a buddy.** Swimming buddies are fun and allow each person to look out for the other in case of danger.
- **Put a gate with a lock around your pool.** This way, your child won't be able to get into the pool without an adult to watch them. Store the key in a safe place.
- **Talk to your child about avoiding alcohol while swimming.** This is especially important for teenagers. Alcohol plays a part in up to half of all teenage and adult drowning accidents in the United States. Make sure you and your children don't drink alcohol near or in any type of water.
- **Learn CPR.** CPR is a lifesaving technique that can help your child or others who are near drowning. Many schools or community centers, like your local YMCA, offer classes to learn CPR.

title: How to Keep Your Child Safe During Your PICU Stay

en.description: A checklist for parents and guardians — ID bracelets, hand hygiene, room safety, and how to spot the care team.

content.markdown:
During a hospital stay, your child's health and safety is the care team's priority. As a parent or guardian, you are also an important part of the care team. Below is a checklist of ways you can help keep your child safe during a hospital stay.

## Identification

- **Make sure your child always wears their ID tag or bracelet.** Let the care team know if the tag or bracelet falls off or gets lost. If your child is 6 months or younger, they will also have a security tag called a **HUGS tag**. Let the care team know if the HUGS tag falls off.
- **Always wear your orange ID bracelet.** This bracelet lets the care team know that you are the parent or guardian. You will receive the bracelet when your child is admitted to the hospital. Let the care team know if the bracelet falls off or gets lost.

## Preventing the spread of germs

- **Before entering your child's room,** wash your hands with soap and water.
- **After using the restroom or changing diapers,** wash your hands with soap and water.

## On the unit

- **Before entering the unit, use the intercom.** A staff member can let you in.
- **Do not hold the doors open for anyone you do not know.**
- **If your child has guests visiting,** ask visitors to use the intercom and check in at the front desk. They should also wear a visitor sticker at all times.

## In the hospital room

- **To prevent falls and injury,** move slowly around your child's crib or bedside and wear non-skid slippers or shoes.
- **If your child feels weak or dizzy,** ask the care team for help before moving your child.
- **Keep the guardrails up on your child's crib or hospital bed,** even if you only turn away or leave the room for a moment.
- **Keep the hospital room free of clutter.** Bring only what you and your child need during the hospital stay. Keep personal items out of the way where people walk.
- **If your child is sharing a hospital room with someone else,** keep your belongings separate from the other family's belongings.

## The care team

- **Know who is on your child's care team.** All staff have a picture ID. You can ask to see a care team member's ID badge at any time.

---

*Revised April 2018. Reviewed by the MGHfC Family Advisory Council.*

content.markdown:
Coming to the Emergency Department can feel scary for children. This short video — *You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED* — gives kids a tour of what to expect when they arrive: the people they'll meet, the rooms they'll see, and what happens at each step.

Watching it together before a visit (or revisiting after one) can help children feel more in control of an unfamiliar experience.

content.caption: You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED — Mass General Hospital

content.markdown:
## About the video

A trip to the Emergency Department is stressful for patients, particularly for children. *You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED* explains what pediatric patients can expect during an emergency room visit and gives children insight into their healthcare experience.

Wendy Wooden and her mother, Darcy Daniels, are very familiar with Mass General for Children's Emergency Department and inpatient units. Wendy was diagnosed at age 3 with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), caused by an E. coli infection, and has a complex medical history including heart failure, kidney and pancreatic damage that required a kidney transplant, and a partial intestinal removal at age 5. Her care has spanned five pediatric subspecialties.

While Wendy is a frequent patient accustomed to beeping machines and procedures, she says she still gets overwhelmed by urgent trips and admissions to the hospital. In 2014 — when a neighbor called for advice about what to expect when her two children were going to be in the hospital — Wendy realized that other children, less experienced with medical treatment, may feel similar anxieties.

With the help of her mother, Wendy wrote *You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED*, a guide for what fellow pediatric patients can expect during an emergency room visit and how to help reduce anxiety and foster communication between their parents and providers.

> "We've learned a lot over the years from the compassionate care we've received from Wendy's team of doctors, nurses, and other staff members. We wanted to share those lessons so other patients and families can get the best care possible while cutting down on stress and worry."
>
> — *Darcy Daniels, Wendy's mother and member of the MGfC Family Advisory Council*

The project gained new life thanks to [Payette](http://www.payette.com/), a Boston-based architecture firm, who transformed the story into an animated video. The nine-minute piece is narrated by Wendy and uses stop-motion animation — in which an image is incrementally altered in individual photos to mimic movement atop altered video of the MGH environment. It provides step-by-step introductions about what to expect during trauma care and highlights the department's child-focused features, including interactive LED lights that help soothe patients and child life specialists.

Working from Wendy's narrative, the Payette team developed the animation concept and storyboard before enlisting the help of over 20 staff members who spent more than 1,000 hours contributing their expertise in drawing, animation, still and time-lapse photography, videography, computer scripting, and video editing to bring the final animation to life.

*Wendy's Welcome* is part of MGfC's efforts to provide a dedicated pediatric space that helps children manage stress while optimizing care during emergency treatment. After nearly five years of designing and planning, the new Pediatric Emergency Department — outfitted with televisions, iPads, and toys — was unveiled in 2015. The area offers a friendly, unintimidating environment with bright artwork and individually themed exam rooms.

> "Our jobs require us to treat acute illness and injury, but as doctors, we also realize the need to address potential stress and anxiety in kids who require an emergency visit here. *Wendy's Welcome to the ED* is one more tool in our educational toy box that we can offer to kids and their families to ease their fears."
>
> — *Ari Cohen, MD, Division Chief, MGfC Pediatric Emergency Medicine*

en.description: How to prepare and support your child during IV placement and bloodwork — by age, with scripts and comfort techniques.

content.markdown:
At Mass General Hospital for Children, we are committed to making your child's IV or blood test as comfortable as possible. Your role is very important — children find it comforting when their parents are involved. This guide will give you some ideas about how you can best help your child.

## What should I tell my child?

Tell your child what is going to happen, and encourage your child to ask questions. You know your child best, and you know how much information your child can take in at a time.

## What can I do for my infant during the procedure?

It is very important to support your infant during the actual procedure. We recommend you:

- **Hold your baby** when possible. Soothing touch, such as rubbing your infant's head or back, also helps.
- **Swaddle your infant snugly** in a blanket so their entire body is covered. This helps your infant feel a sense of control.
- **Breastfeed your infant.** It is a familiar source of comfort and helps to distract your baby.
- **Give specially prepared sucrose (Sweet Ease).** Ask the staff if you are interested in this.
- **Distract your infant.** Talk and smile with younger infants, and play with older infants.

## How to answer your child's questions about the test or procedure

**Why do I need this done?**

The blood test will give the doctor information to help take care of you. Having an IV placed helps to give you important liquid or medicine that you can't swallow.

**What will happen to me?**

- They will clean the area where you need the blood test or IV. This will feel cool and may have a funny smell.
- A big rubber band called a tourniquet will be wrapped around your arm, giving your arm a tight hug.

**What should I do during the test?**

Your job is to hold still. It is OK to cry, but holding still will make the test go more quickly.

- They will tap on your arm to find veins. Veins are the small blue lines under your skin — the roads our blood uses to travel through the body.
- An IV is like a small straw that goes in your vein. The needle helps get the straw in, and will come out when the straw is in the vein.

> Be honest about the needle, but let your child know the needle will not be in for too long.

## What can I do for my child during the procedure?

**Distraction.** Distraction is the best way to calm your child. Pick something that will hold your child's attention — music, reading, blowing bubbles, talking (not about the hospital), or counting.

**Imagery.** Have your child think about a happy time. Talk about a memory, like a fun vacation, going down a roller coaster, or hitting a home run. You can help them get into the details — what were the sounds and smells around them, who else was there, and what it would be like if they did it again.

**Holding.** Many children like their parents to hold them during the procedure. If your child is young, they may want to sit on your lap. An older child may prefer you to hold their hand or rub their back.

## What can I do if I will not be with my child during a procedure?

Some parents prefer not to be with their child during a needle stick. There are also times when a child is hospitalized and parents are unable to make arrangements to be with their child. The staff will work with you to plan the best ways to help your child when you are not able to be there.

## Numbing medicine

There are local anesthetics or "numbing" medicines, which may make the *poke* hurt less. Some work quickly; others take a half hour to an hour to work. Many children like to use numbing medicine, but some children do not want to wait. Talk with your provider about the use of local anesthetics for your child. Make sure your child knows that they will feel some pressure during the procedure, even with the medicine.

## Praise and rewards

Praising your child right after the procedure is very important. If your child feels good about how it went, they are more likely to do well with other medical tests they may have. Let your child know they did well. Rewards like stickers or a special treat let your child know they have done a good job.

## Working with a child life specialist

A child life specialist is trained in preparing and supporting children and parents through medical tests. They can answer any questions that you have about how to best help your child. Tell your child's doctor or nurse if you would like to meet with a child life specialist.

## Let us know…

It is very helpful for us to know about your child's past experiences with blood tests and IV insertions. If these procedures have gone well in the past, let us know what worked. If your child has had difficulty tolerating these procedures, we will work with you and your child to improve the experience. Let us know if there have been any problems finding your child's veins in the past. Child life specialists are especially helpful for children who need additional preparation, help, and support.

content.markdown:
## Contact Information

**Critical Care Medicine / PICU**

Boston, MA 02114
